options.text: Yes: both classes have the same instance shape, so a Cat is assignable to Dog
options.why: TypeScript compares class instances by their members, not by the class name.

options.text: No: Cat and Dog are different classes, so TypeScript reports a nominal type mismatch
options.why: That is how Java or C# behave. TypeScript is structural, so names do not matter here.

options.text: No: assigning a class instance needs an explicit `as Dog` cast to change its type
options.why: No cast is needed when the shapes already match; casts are for when they do not.

options.text: Only if Cat is declared with `extends Dog`, which makes Cat a subtype of Dog
options.why: Inheritance is one way to match shapes, but it is not required; matching members is enough.

explanation: TypeScript uses structural typing: a type is compatible with another if it has at least the required members with compatible types. `Dog` and `Cat` both have exactly `name: string`, so the assignment compiles. Private and protected members are the main exception, covered in other questions.

options.text: Both calls, because `z` is not a property of `Point`
options.why: Extra properties are only an error on a fresh object literal, not on a variable.

options.text: Only call 2, the object literal written directly at the call site
options.why: Fresh object literals get an excess property check, so the unexpected `z` is flagged.

options.text: Only call 1, because `pt` was inferred with an extra `z` property
options.why: A variable with extra properties is still structurally a valid `Point`.

options.text: Neither call, because both values have the `x` and `y` that `Point` requires
options.why: Structurally both values fit, but the literal also triggers the excess property check.

explanation: Excess property checking applies only to "fresh" object literals assigned or passed directly to a typed target. tsc reports: "Object literal may only specify known properties, and 'z' does not exist in type 'Point'." The variable `pt` is not fresh, so call 1 is accepted structurally. The check exists to catch typos in literals, not to forbid extra data.

stem: If you declare `interface User { name: string }` and later, in the same scope, `interface User { age: number }`, TypeScript merges them into one interface that requires both `name` and `age`.

options.text: True
options.why: Interfaces are open: declarations with the same name in the same scope merge their members.

options.text: False
options.why: This is declaration merging, a documented feature of interfaces; only type aliases reject a second declaration.

explanation: Interface declaration merging combines members from every declaration with the same name. An object typed `User` must then have both properties: assigning `{ name: "a" }` errors with "Property 'age' is missing". Type aliases cannot merge; declaring the same alias twice is a "Duplicate identifier" error. Merging is how libraries let you augment types like `Window`.

options.text: Nothing: `readonly` only stops you from reassigning the variable `a` itself
options.why: That describes `const`. `readonly number[]` restricts the array's contents too.

options.text: An error: `push` does not exist on type `readonly number[]`
options.why: Readonly array types drop every mutating method, such as push, pop and splice.

options.text: A runtime TypeError, because the array is frozen when the code runs
options.why: Readonly is compile-time only. Nothing is frozen at runtime unless you call `Object.freeze`.

options.text: An error saying that a readonly array cannot be created from an array literal
options.why: Initialising a readonly array from a literal is fine; only mutation is blocked.

explanation: `readonly number[]` (also written `ReadonlyArray<number>`) is a type without mutating methods. tsc reports "Property 'push' does not exist on type 'readonly number[]'." It is a compile-time guarantee only: the emitted JavaScript is an ordinary array.

stem: Which TypeScript modifier, placed before a property name in an interface, makes the compiler reject any assignment to that property after the object is created? Type the keyword.
explanation: `readonly` marks a property as not assignable through that type, for example `interface Config { readonly url: string }`. It is checked only at compile time and only through that type: an alias with a mutable type can still change it, as another question shows.

stem:
With `strict: true`, which line is an error?

```ts
let a: {} = 'hello';  // line 1
let b: {} = 42;       // line 2
let c: {} = null;     // line 3
let d: {} = [1];      // line 4
```

options.text: Lines 1 and 2, because `{}` means "an object" and strings and numbers are primitives
options.why: Primitives have properties through their wrappers, so they fit the empty object type.

options.text: Only line 3, because `{}` accepts every value except `null` and `undefined`
options.why: Under strictNullChecks, null and undefined are the only values excluded from `{}`.

options.text: Only line 4, because an array has more members than the empty type allows
options.why: Extra members are fine structurally, and this is not a fresh object literal check.

options.text: None of them, because `{}` is the top type and behaves exactly like `unknown`
options.why: `unknown` also admits null and undefined; `{}` does not under strict mode.

explanation: The empty object type `{}` requires no members, so any value that is not `null` or `undefined` is assignable, including strings and numbers. tsc reports "Type 'null' is not assignable to type '{}'." on line 3. Use `object` for "any non-primitive" and `Record<string, unknown>` for "a plain dictionary".

stem: Which two statements about interfaces and type aliases are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Only a type alias can name a union such as `type Id = string | number`
options.why: Interfaces always describe a single object shape; unions need a type alias.

options.text: An interface can extend a type alias, as long as the alias is an object type
options.why: For example `type T = { a: string }; interface I extends T {}` compiles.

options.text: A class can implement an interface, but it can never implement a type alias
options.why: A class can implement an object type alias too; only unions are rejected.

options.text: Declaring a type alias twice merges both declarations, just like interfaces
options.why: A second alias with the same name is a "Duplicate identifier" error.

options.text: Interfaces can describe functions and tuples, but type aliases cannot
options.why: Type aliases describe functions and tuples easily, for example `type Fn = (x: number) => string`.

explanation: Both describe object shapes and mostly interoperate. Differences: aliases can name unions, primitives, tuples and mapped or conditional types; interfaces merge across declarations and give clearer error messages for object hierarchies. An interface can extend an object type alias, but `interface J extends (A | B)` errors: "An interface can only extend an object type or intersection of object types with statically known members."
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Differences Between Type Aliases and Interfaces

stem:
Which assignment is an error under `strict: true`?

```ts
declare const maybe: { a?: number };

const o1: { a?: number } = {};            // 1
const o2: { a: number } = maybe;          // 2
const o3: { a?: number } = { a: 1 };      // 3
const o4: { a?: number } = { a: undefined }; // 4
```

options.text: Assignment 1, because an empty object does not have the property `a`
options.why: An optional property may be absent, so `{}` is a valid value.

options.text: Assignment 2, because an optional property cannot satisfy a required one
options.why: The source may lack `a`, but the target promises that `a` is always a number.

options.text: Assignment 4, because `undefined` can never be written into an optional property
options.why: Without exactOptionalPropertyTypes, an optional property also accepts undefined.

options.text: Assignments 1 and 4, since optional properties must be omitted or set to a number
options.why: Both are accepted under default strict settings; only the flag discussed elsewhere changes 4.

explanation: Optional (`a?: number`) to required (`a: number`) fails because the value might not have `a`: tsc reports "Type '{ a?: number | undefined; }' is not assignable to type '{ a: number; }'." The reverse direction is fine. Under default strict settings `a?: number` reads as `number | undefined`, so writing `undefined` is allowed; `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` changes that.

options.text: Nothing: named properties always take priority over the index signature
options.why: Named properties must still conform to a string index signature.

options.text: An error: property `count` of type `string` is not assignable to the `string` index type `number`
options.why: Every named property is also reachable as `dict["count"]`, so it must fit the index type.

options.text: An error: interfaces cannot mix index signatures with named properties
options.why: Mixing them is common; the named properties just have to fit the signature.

options.text: Nothing at declaration, but every read of `count` is typed `number`
options.why: The declaration itself is rejected; TypeScript does not silently retype the property.

explanation: A string index signature describes every string key, including named ones. tsc reports "Property 'count' of type 'string' is not assignable to 'string' index type 'number'." Fix it by widening the signature, for example `[key: string]: number | string`, or by moving the dictionary into its own property.

stem: Match each type with the values it accepts under `strict: true`.

options.text: Any value, and you must narrow it before using it
options.why: The safe top type.

options.text: Any value, and every operation on it is allowed without checks
options.why: Turns checking off.

options.text: No value at all
options.why: The bottom type.

options.text: Any value except null and undefined
options.why: Includes primitives.

explanation: `unknown` and `any` both accept everything, but `unknown` forces you to narrow before use, while `any` disables checking in both directions. `never` has no values, which is why it appears for impossible cases and exhaustive checks. `{}` is "anything non-nullish", which surprises people who expect it to mean "an empty object".
reference: TypeScript Handbook: unknown, never and object types

stem: Under `strict: true`, a value of type `unknown` can be assigned to a variable of type `string` without narrowing or an assertion.

options.text: True
options.why: `unknown` is assignable only to `unknown` and `any`; anything else needs narrowing first.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: tsc reports "Type 'unknown' is not assignable to type 'string'."

explanation: `unknown` is the type-safe top type: everything is assignable to it, but it is assignable only to `unknown` and `any`. Use a check such as `typeof u === "string"` to narrow it first. `any` is the opposite: it is assignable to almost everything, which is why it is unsafe.

options.text: Lines 1 and 3, because both pass an object with an unknown `retries` property
options.why: Line 1 passes a variable, which is not fresh, so it is not checked for extras.

options.text: Lines 3 and 4, because both build a new object literal containing `retries`
options.why: Properties that come from a spread are not checked for excess, so line 4 is accepted.

options.text: Only line 3
options.why: It is the only fresh literal that spells out the extra property without an assertion.

options.text: Lines 2 and 3, because an assertion cannot hide a property the type does not declare
options.why: An `as` assertion is allowed when the types are comparable, and it skips the excess check.

explanation: Excess property checks run only on fresh object literals with explicit properties. A variable (line 1) has lost freshness; an assertion (line 2) replaces the check with a comparability check; properties brought in by a spread (line 4) are not checked. Only line 3 is reported: "Object literal may only specify known properties, and 'retries' does not exist in type 'Opts'."

options.text: Yes, because `size` exists on one member of the union, so it is a known property
options.why: That rule applies to unions without a discriminant; here the `kind` picks one member.

options.text: No: `kind: 'circle'` selects the circle member, and `size` is excess for it
options.why: With a discriminant, TypeScript checks the literal against the matching member only.

options.text: No, because an object literal can never be assigned to a union type directly
options.why: Literals are assigned to unions all the time; the problem is the extra property.

options.text: Yes, but `s.size` is then typed `number | undefined` everywhere
options.why: The literal is rejected, so the question of how `s.size` is typed never arises.

explanation: For a discriminated union, the literal's discriminant narrows the target before the excess property check. tsc reports "Object literal may only specify known properties, and 'size' does not exist in type '{ kind: "circle"; r: number; }'." Without a discriminant, TypeScript is more lenient, as another question shows.

stem:
Which line is an error?

```ts
const m: number[] = [1];
const r: readonly number[] = m;  // line 2
const w: number[] = r;           // line 3
```

options.text: Line 2, because a mutable array cannot be stored in a readonly variable
options.why: Mutable to readonly is safe: you only lose the ability to mutate through `r`.

options.text: Line 3, because a readonly array cannot be assigned to a mutable array type
options.why: Allowing it would let `w.push` mutate an array that was promised to be read-only.

options.text: Both lines, because readonly and mutable arrays are unrelated types
options.why: They are related one way: mutable is a subtype of readonly.

options.text: Neither line, because both variables point to the same array at runtime
options.why: Runtime identity does not matter; the compiler checks the declared types.

explanation: `number[]` is assignable to `readonly number[]`, but not the other way round. tsc reports "The type 'readonly number[]' is 'readonly' and cannot be assigned to the mutable type 'number[]'." This lets functions accept `readonly T[]` parameters and still be called with ordinary arrays.

stem:
What happens with these declarations?

```ts
interface A { x: string }
interface B extends A { x: number }  // declaration 1
type C = A & { x: number };          // declaration 2
```

options.text: Both are errors, because `x` cannot be both a string and a number
options.why: An intersection never errors at its declaration; it silently computes a type.

options.text: Both compile, and `B['x']` and `C['x']` are both `string & number`
options.why: The interface is checked against its base and fails; it does not intersect.

options.text: Declaration 1 errors; declaration 2 compiles, and `C['x']` is `never`
options.why: `extends` checks compatibility with the base, while `&` combines the property types.

options.text: Declaration 1 compiles because `x` is overridden, and declaration 2 errors
options.why: Interfaces cannot override a property with an incompatible type.

explanation: An interface that extends another must stay assignable to it. tsc reports "Interface 'B' incorrectly extends interface 'A'." An intersection instead merges the property types: `string & number` is `never`, so `C` is a type whose `x` can never be satisfied. That silent `never` is one reason interfaces give better errors for hierarchies.
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Extending Types vs Intersections

stem: Two interfaces named `Settings` are declared in the same file. Which two statements about how TypeScript merges them are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: If both declare a non-method property with different types, TypeScript reports an error
options.why: tsc: "Subsequent property declarations must have the same type."

options.text: If both declare a method with the same name, the methods become overloads
options.why: Merged function members turn into an overload list.

options.text: The later declaration silently replaces any property with the same name
options.why: Conflicts are errors, not overrides; nothing is replaced silently.

options.text: An interface and a type alias with the same name merge in the same way
options.why: An alias cannot share a name with an interface; that is a duplicate identifier.

options.text: Merging only happens across files, never within a single file
options.why: Merging happens in any shared scope, including one file.

explanation: Interface merging adds members from each declaration. Non-function members with the same name must have identical types, or tsc reports "Subsequent property declarations must have the same type. Property 'a' must be of type 'string', but here has type 'number'." Methods with the same name become overloads, and later declarations' overloads are listed first.

options.text: Nothing: `input` is not a fresh literal, so extra properties are allowed
options.why: This is a different check that also applies to non-fresh values.

options.text: An error: `{ verbos: boolean }` has no properties in common with `Options`
options.why: This is weak type detection, for types whose properties are all optional.

options.text: An error: `verbose` is missing in `{ verbos: boolean }`
options.why: Nothing is missing: every property of `Options` is optional.

options.text: Nothing, because every property of `Options` is optional, so any object fits
options.why: That loophole is exactly what weak type detection closes.

explanation: A "weak type" has only optional properties. Since TypeScript 2.4, assigning a value that shares none of those properties is an error, even for non-fresh values: "Type '{ verbos: boolean; }' has no properties in common with type 'Options'." It catches typos like `verbos` that would otherwise slip through structural typing.
reference: TypeScript 2.4 release notes: Weak Type Detection

stem: Given `type X = { a: string } & { a: number };`, what type is `X['a']`? Type the type.
explanation: Intersecting two object types intersects the types of properties with the same name: `string & number` has no values, so it reduces to `never`. `X` itself is not `never` (it is still an object type), but no value can ever satisfy it. When the conflicting properties are literal discriminants, TypeScript reduces the whole intersection to `never`.

stem: Order these types from widest (accepts the most values) to narrowest. Each type should be assignable to every type above it.

options.text: `unknown`
options.why: Accepts every value.
Every value except null and undefined.

options.text: `{ a: string }`
options.why: Objects with a string `a`.

options.text: `{ a: 'x'; b: number }`
options.why: A narrower `a` plus a required `b`.

options.text: `never`
options.why: No values at all.

explanation: Each step adds requirements. `never` is assignable to everything; `{ a: 'x'; b: number }` is assignable to `{ a: string }` because `'x'` fits `string` and extra properties are allowed; that fits `{}`; and everything fits `unknown`. None of the reverse assignments compiles: for example `unknown` to `{}` errors with "Type 'unknown' is not assignable to type '{}'."

stem:
Which line is an error?

```ts
const t: [number, string] = [1, 'a'];
const arr: (number | string)[] = t;   // line 2
const back: [number, string] = arr;   // line 3
```

options.text: Line 2, because a tuple has a fixed length and an array does not
options.why: A tuple is a special array, so it fits the wider element-union array type.

options.text: Line 3, because an array of unknown length cannot satisfy a fixed tuple
options.why: The array might be empty or have the elements in a different order.

options.text: Both lines, because tuples and arrays are never mutually assignable
options.why: Tuple to array works; only array to tuple fails.

options.text: Neither, because `back` gets exactly the same values that `t` had
options.why: The compiler checks types, and `arr`'s type has lost the tuple's length and order.

explanation: `[number, string]` is assignable to `(number | string)[]` because every element fits the union. The reverse fails because `(number | string)[]` says nothing about length or position: "Type '(string | number)[]' is not assignable to type '[number, string]'." Use `as const` or an explicit tuple type to keep tuple information.

stem: Because `any` turns off type checking, `const n: never = value as any;` compiles.

options.text: True
options.why: `any` is assignable to every type except `never`; this assignment is rejected.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: tsc reports "Type 'any' is not assignable to type 'never'."

explanation: `any` is assignable to every other type, with one exception: `never`. That keeps `never` meaningful, so exhaustiveness checks like `const _exhaustive: never = shape;` are not silently defeated by an `any` value.

stem:
Which assignment is an error?

```ts
type Handler = (event: string, attempt: number) => void;

const h1: Handler = (event) => {};                    // 1
const h2: Handler = () => {};                         // 2
const h3: Handler = (e: string, a: number, extra: boolean) => {}; // 3
```

options.text: Assignments 1 and 2, because they ignore parameters the caller will pass
options.why: Ignoring extra arguments is safe and common, as in `arr.forEach((x) => ...)`.

options.text: Only assignment 3, because it requires a third argument callers never pass
options.why: A function with more required parameters cannot stand in for one with fewer.

options.text: Only assignment 2, because a handler must declare at least one parameter
options.why: Zero parameters is the simplest valid implementation.

options.text: None of them, because extra parameters are always ignored at runtime
options.why: At runtime `extra` would be undefined, which is exactly what the check prevents.

explanation: A function with fewer parameters is assignable to a function type with more, because JavaScript ignores extra arguments. A function that needs more parameters than the type supplies is not: "Type '(e: string, a: number, extra: boolean) => void' is not assignable to type 'Handler'." This is why callbacks like `forEach` can take just the element.

stem: Match each tsc error message with the situation that produces it.

options.text: A fresh object literal has a property the target type does not declare
options.why: Excess property check.

options.text: A value shares none of the properties of an all-optional type
options.why: Weak type detection.

options.text: A `readonly T[]` value is assigned to a `T[]` variable
options.why: Readonly to mutable.

options.text: A value lacks a property that the target type requires
options.why: Missing required member.

prompts.text: "Object literal may only specify known properties"
"Type … has no properties in common with type …"
"… is 'readonly' and cannot be assigned to the mutable type …"
"Property 'x' is missing in type … but required in type …"

explanation: Recognising these four messages speeds up debugging. Excess property errors only appear on literals; weak type errors appear even on variables; the readonly message points at array or tuple mutability; and "missing" errors mean the source lacks a required member.

stem:
Which line does TypeScript reject?

```ts
interface Box { readonly v: number }

const m = { v: 1 };
const b: Box = m;               // 1
m.v = 2;                        // 2
const back: { v: number } = b;  // 3
back.v = 3;                     // 4
b.v = 4;                        // 5
```

options.text: Lines 1 and 3, because readonly and mutable properties are incompatible
options.why: `readonly` on a property does not affect assignability in either direction.

options.text: Lines 2, 4 and 5, because `b` was declared readonly
options.why: `m` and `back` have mutable types, so writes through them are allowed.

options.text: Only line 5
options.why: Only writes through the `Box` type are checked; the same object is mutable through other aliases.

options.text: Lines 3 and 5, because once a value is typed readonly it can never become mutable again
options.why: Unlike readonly arrays, readonly properties can be assigned to mutable types.

explanation: Property-level `readonly` only stops writes through that particular type. It is not considered in assignability, so `{ v: number }` and `{ readonly v: number }` are mutually assignable. Here `b.v` ends up 3 at runtime despite `Box` being readonly, because lines 2 and 4 mutate it through aliases. Readonly arrays are different: `readonly T[]` to `T[]` is rejected.

stem:
Which assignment is an error?

```ts
type AorB = { a: number } | { b: string };

const x: AorB = { a: 1, b: 'two' };  // 1
const y: AorB = { a: 1, c: true };   // 2
```

options.text: Both, because each literal has a property that one of the union members lacks
options.why: For non-discriminated unions, a property is known if any member declares it.

options.text: Only assignment 1, because a value cannot match both union members at once
options.why: Matching both members is fine: unions are not exclusive in TypeScript.

options.text: Only assignment 2, because `c` is not declared by any union member
options.why: The excess property check accepts properties declared anywhere in the union.

options.text: Neither, because excess property checks are disabled for union targets
options.why: They still run, with the looser rule; `c` is flagged.

explanation: Without a discriminant, excess property checking treats a property as known if any union member declares it. So `{ a: 1, b: 'two' }` passes, even though it matches both members, while `c` is reported: "Object literal may only specify known properties, and 'c' does not exist in type 'AorB'." If you need "exactly one of", add a discriminant or use `{ a: number; b?: never } | { a?: never; b: string }`.

options.text: Both lines, because a Dog handler cannot safely receive every Animal
options.why: That would be the sound answer, but methods are deliberately exempt.

options.text: Only line 2, because only function-typed properties get strict parameter checks
options.why: Methods declared with method syntax compare parameters bivariantly.

options.text: Only line 1, because method syntax is checked more strictly than property syntax
options.why: It is the other way round: method syntax is the lenient one.

options.text: Neither line, because `strictFunctionTypes` only applies to standalone function types
options.why: It applies to function-typed properties too, which is why line 2 fails.

explanation: `strictFunctionTypes` checks parameters contravariantly for function types, including properties written as `handle: (a: Animal) => void`. Method syntax `handle(a: Animal): void` stays bivariant for compatibility with existing code such as DOM APIs. So line 2 reports "Type '(d: Dog) => void' is not assignable to type '(a: Animal) => void'", while line 1 compiles and can crash if `m.handle` receives a plain Animal.

options.text: It returns "woof", because TypeScript converted the Animal to a Dog when it was pushed
options.why: TypeScript never converts values; types are erased before the code runs.

options.text: It throws a TypeError, because `dogs[1]` is a plain Animal with no `bark` method
options.why: Arrays are checked covariantly, which is unsound for writes through the wider alias.

options.text: It returns undefined, because a missing method call on an object returns undefined
options.why: Calling a missing method calls `undefined`, which throws.

options.text: It never runs: the push is a compile error once the array is aliased
options.why: The compiler accepts it; that is the point of the question.

explanation: TypeScript treats `Dog[]` as assignable to `Animal[]` (array covariance). That is convenient for reads, but writing through the `Animal[]` alias puts an Animal into the Dog array. At runtime `dogs[1].bark` is undefined, so the call throws "TypeError: dogs[1].bark is not a function". Accepting `readonly Animal[]` in APIs avoids the problem, since readonly arrays cannot be written to.
reference: TypeScript FAQ: Why are function parameters bivariant / array covariance

options.text: Only line 1, because classes with private members compare by name
options.why: Line 3 also fails: a plain object cannot supply A's private member.

options.text: Lines 1 and 3
options.why: A private member is only compatible with the same declaration, so B and the literal both fail.

options.text: Lines 1, 2 and 3, because classes are always compared nominally
options.why: P1 and P2 are compatible: they only have public members.

options.text: None, because `private` is erased at runtime and ignored by the type checker
options.why: It is erased at runtime, but the checker still uses it for compatibility.

explanation: A `private` or `protected` member makes compatibility nominal for that member: it must come from the same declaration. Line 1 reports "Type 'B' is not assignable to type 'A'. Types have separate declarations of a private property 'x'." Line 3 fails because 'x' is private in A but not in the literal. Line 2 compiles because public members are compared structurally.
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Private and Protected Members in Classes

stem: Which three declarations compile under `strict: true` without `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`? (Choose three.)

options.text: `interface N1 { [i: number]: string; [s: string]: string }`
options.why: The number index type must be assignable to the string index type, and it is.

options.text: `interface N2 { [i: number]: number; [s: string]: string }`
options.why: Error: 'number' index type 'number' is not assignable to 'string' index type 'string'.

options.text: `interface N3 { [k: string]: number; length?: number }`
options.why: Error: the optional property has type number | undefined, which does not fit the index type.

options.text: `interface N4 { [k: string]: number | undefined; length?: number }`
options.why: Including undefined in the index type makes the optional property fit.

options.text: `const d: Record<string, number> = {}; const v: number = d.missing;`
options.why: Without the flag, index reads are typed as the value type with no undefined.

explanation: Numeric keys are converted to strings in JavaScript, so a number index signature must be a subtype of the string one. Optional properties read as `T | undefined`, which must fit a string index signature. And by default `d.missing` is typed `number` even though it is undefined at runtime; `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` adds `| undefined` to such reads.

options.text: `string | undefined`, `number | undefined`, `string | undefined`, `string | undefined`
options.why: Iteration and known tuple positions are not affected by the flag.

options.text: `string | undefined`, `number | undefined`, `string`, `string`
options.why: Only index reads that might miss get `| undefined`; `for...of` and fixed tuple slots do not.

options.text: `string`, `number | undefined`, `string`, `string`
options.why: Array element reads are index reads too, so `arr[0]` also gets `| undefined`.

options.text: `string | undefined`, `number`, `string`, `string`
options.why: `Record<string, number>` has a string index signature, so it is affected too.

explanation: `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` adds `| undefined` to reads through index signatures, including array element access, because the key might not exist. Values produced by iteration cannot be missing, so `s` stays `string`, and a tuple's declared position `tup[0]` is known to exist, so it stays `string`. The flag is not part of `strict`; you enable it separately.

stem: Under `strictFunctionTypes`, a function of type `(x: string) => void` can be assigned to a variable of type `(x: string | number) => void`.

options.text: True
options.why: Callers could then pass a number to a function that only handles strings.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: function type parameters are checked contravariantly, so the narrower parameter is rejected.

explanation: A variable of type `(x: string | number) => void` may be called with a number. A function that only accepts strings would receive a value it cannot handle, so tsc reports "Type '(x: string) => void' is not assignable to type '(x: string | number) => void'." The opposite direction compiles: a function that accepts `string | number` can stand in for one that is only ever given strings.

stem: Given `type K = { kind: 'a'; v: string } & { kind: 'b' };`, what does TypeScript reduce the whole type `K` to? Type the type.
explanation: Since TypeScript 3.9, an intersection of object types whose shared property has disjoint literal types (a discriminant) reduces entirely to `never`, not just the property. `{ kind: 'a' } & { kind: 'b' }` can never exist. In contrast, `{ a: string } & { a: number }` stays an object type whose `a` is `never`.
reference: TypeScript 3.9 release notes: Intersections Reduced By Discriminant Properties

options.text: Only line 1, because every branded string is interchangeable once it has been cast
options.why: Different brands have incompatible `__brand` literal types.

options.text: Lines 1, 3 and 4, because a branded value is no longer usable as a string
options.why: A brand is `string & {...}`, so all string members remain available.

options.text: Lines 1 and 3
options.why: A plain string lacks the brand, and OrderId's brand is the wrong literal.

options.text: Lines 2 and 3, because the `as` cast must be checked against the brand at runtime
options.why: Casts are not checked at runtime; the brand exists only in the type system.

explanation: Branding fakes nominal typing in a structural system: the phantom `__brand` property makes `UserId` and `OrderId` incompatible with each other and with plain `string`. Line 1: "Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'UserId'." Line 3: "Argument of type 'OrderId' is not assignable...". The brand costs nothing at runtime; create branded values in one validating function rather than casting everywhere.
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Type Compatibility (nominal typing workarounds)

stem:
Given `interface Cfg { port: number }`, which three lines report an excess property error for `host`? (Choose three.)

```ts
function make(): Cfg { return { port: 1, host: 'x' }; }          // 1
const viaFn: () => Cfg = () => ({ port: 1, host: 'x' });         // 2
const list: Cfg[] = [{ port: 1, host: 'x' }];                    // 3
const nested: { cfg: Cfg } = { cfg: { port: 1, host: 'x' } };    // 4
const extra = { host: 'x' };
const spread: Cfg = { port: 1, ...extra };                       // 5
```

options.text: Line 1
options.why: A literal returned from a function with a declared return type is checked.

options.text: Line 2
options.why: The arrow's return type is inferred from the literal, then the function types are compared, so no excess check runs.

options.text: Line 3
options.why: Literals inside an array literal are fresh too.

options.text: Line 4
options.why: Nested object literals are checked against the nested property type.

options.text: Line 5
options.why: Properties that arrive through a spread are not checked for excess.

explanation: Freshness follows the literal wherever it is directly checked against a declared type: return statements of annotated functions, array elements and nested properties. Two common gaps: an arrow function assigned to a function type infers its own return type first, so line 2 compiles (annotate `(): Cfg =>` to get the check), and spread properties are never treated as excess.

stem: Order these array and tuple types from widest to narrowest, so that each is assignable to every type above it.

options.text: `readonly (string | number)[]`
options.why: Read-only, any length.

options.text: `(string | number)[]`
options.why: Mutable, any length.

options.text: `[string, number]`
options.why: Fixed length and positions.

options.text: `[string, 42]`
options.why: Fixed, with a literal second element.

explanation: A tuple is assignable to an array of the union of its elements; a mutable array is assignable to a readonly one; and a tuple with a literal element is assignable to one with the wider element type. The reverse steps all fail, for example "The type 'readonly (string | number)[]' is 'readonly' and cannot be assigned to the mutable type '(string | number)[]'."
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Tuple Types and ReadonlyArray

options.text: `n` is undefined, because the optional chain stops when `b` is not a number
options.why: Optional chaining only stops on null or undefined, and `b` is the string 'text'.

options.text: It throws a TypeError: widening to `{ a: number }` forgot `b`, and an absent optional `b` is accepted
options.why: Each step is allowed alone, but together they relabel a string as a number.

options.text: It never compiles: TypeScript tracks that `b` is a string through both assignments
options.why: Assignments use the declared type; the earlier type of `b` is forgotten.

options.text: `n` is "text", because `toFixed` falls back to the string when called on one
options.why: Strings have no `toFixed` method, so the call throws.

explanation: Step 1 is ordinary width subtyping: `{ a; b: string }` to `{ a: number }` drops knowledge of `b`. Step 2 allows a source without `b` to fill a target where `b?: number` is optional. Each rule is reasonable, but composed they are unsound: at runtime `opt.b` is 'text', so `opt.b?.toFixed` is undefined and calling it throws "TypeError: opt.b?.toFixed is not a function". This is a known, accepted hole in structural typing.
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Type Compatibility (A Note on Soundness)

options.text: Assignment 1, because a type alias of an object literal type has no index signature
options.why: Object literal types get an implicit index signature, so 1 compiles.

options.text: Only assignment 2, because interfaces do not get an implicit index signature
options.why: An interface could gain more members through merging, so TypeScript will not assume one.

options.text: Assignments 1 and 2, because neither declares `[key: string]: string`
options.why: Only the interface is rejected; the alias is given an implicit index signature.

options.text: Assignment 3, because `object` excludes interfaces with only primitive members
options.why: `object` accepts any non-primitive, so an IPerson fits.

explanation: Identical shapes, different results: tsc reports "Type 'IPerson' is not assignable to type 'Record<string, string>'. Index signature for type 'string' is missing in type 'IPerson'." Types written as object literal type aliases receive an implicit index signature; interfaces do not, because declaration merging could add members of other types later. This shows up when passing interfaces to helpers typed `Record<string, unknown>`.
reference: TypeScript GitHub issue #15300: Index signature is missing in type (only on interfaces)

options.text: Line 1
options.why: Each `#x` is a distinct member, so A and B are incompatible.

options.text: Line 2
options.why: Sub inherits Base's protected `id` from the same declaration.

options.text: Line 3
options.why: Other declares its own protected `id`, which is a separate declaration.

options.text: Line 4
options.why: A public `id` cannot stand in for a protected one.

options.text: Line 5
options.why: An interface with the same name merges its members into the class instance type.

explanation: ECMAScript `#private` fields, `private` and `protected` members all require the member to originate from the same declaration, which makes those classes nominal in practice. Subclasses inherit the original declaration, so line 2 compiles. Line 4 fails because 'id' is protected in Base but public in Pub. Line 5 shows class and interface merging: the interface adds `extra` to the instance type (without any runtime value, so it is undefined unless something sets it).
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Classes and Declaration Merging

stem:
With `strict: true` and `exactOptionalPropertyTypes: true`, which lines are errors?

```ts
interface Prefs { theme?: 'dark' | 'light' }

const p1: Prefs = {};                                  // 1
const p2: Prefs = { theme: undefined };                // 2
function reset(p: Prefs) { p.theme = undefined; }      // 3
function clear(p: Prefs) { delete p.theme; }           // 4
```

options.text: Lines 1 and 4, because the flag requires every optional property to be present
options.why: The flag still allows the property to be absent; it forbids writing undefined.

options.text: Lines 2 and 3
options.why: Under the flag, "optional" means "may be missing", not "may hold undefined".

options.text: Only line 4, because deleting a declared property is unsafe
options.why: Deleting an optional property is allowed; it makes the property absent.

options.text: None: the flag only changes how optional properties are read
options.why: It changes writes: undefined is no longer an accepted value for `theme`.

explanation: `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` separates "absent" from "present but undefined". Line 2: "Type '{ theme: undefined; }' is not assignable to type 'Prefs' with 'exactOptionalPropertyTypes: true'." Line 3: "Type 'undefined' is not assignable to type '"dark" | "light"'". Omitting it or deleting it is fine. This matters for code that distinguishes `'theme' in p` from `p.theme === undefined`. Declare `theme?: Theme | undefined` to allow both.

stem:
Given `interface Cfg { port: number }` and `declare const cond: boolean;`, which three lines report an excess property error for `host`? (Choose three.)

```ts
const viaVar = { port: 2, host: 'y' };
const t1: Cfg = cond ? { port: 1 } : viaVar;                 // 1
const paren: Cfg = ({ port: 1, host: 'x' });                // 2
const asserted: Cfg = <Cfg>{ port: 1, host: 'x' };          // 3
const sat = { port: 1, host: 'x' } satisfies Cfg;           // 4
const frozen: Cfg = { port: 1, host: 'x' } as const;        // 5
```

options.text: Line 1
options.why: The branch that carries `host` is a variable, which is not fresh.

options.text: Line 2
options.why: Parentheses do not remove freshness; the literal is still checked.

options.text: Line 3
options.why: A type assertion to `Cfg` replaces the excess check with a comparability check.

options.text: Line 4
options.why: `satisfies` checks the literal against the type, including excess properties.

options.text: Line 5
options.why: `as const` is not an assertion to another type; the readonly literal is still fresh against `Cfg`.

explanation: Parentheses keep a literal fresh (line 2). `satisfies` validates a literal against a type without changing its inferred type, and it reports excess properties (line 4). A const assertion only makes the literal readonly with literal types, so the annotated target still checks it (line 5). An assertion to the target type (line 3) skips the check, and a variable in a conditional branch (line 1) is not fresh, so neither is reported.
reference: TypeScript 4.9 release notes: The satisfies Operator

stem:
Which line is an error?

```ts
type Cb = () => void;

const cb: Cb = () => 42;                              // 1
const r = cb();                                       // 2: r is void
function g(): void { return 42; }                     // 3
const nums: number[] = [];
[1, 2].forEach((n) => nums.push(n));                  // 4
const fv: () => void = function () { return 'x'; };   // 5
```

options.text: Lines 1, 3 and 5, because each returns a value where void is expected
options.why: Only a function declared with a void return type is checked this way.

options.text: Line 4, because `push` returns a number but the callback should return void
options.why: This is the reason the rule exists: callbacks typed void may return anything.

options.text: Only line 3
options.why: An explicit `: void` annotation on a function forbids returning a value.

options.text: Lines 3 and 5, because function expressions are checked like declarations
options.why: Line 5 is assigned to a `() => void` type, so its return value is simply ignored.

explanation: A function type with a `void` return means "the caller will ignore the result", so any function is assignable to it. That is why `forEach((n) => nums.push(n))` compiles even though `push` returns a number. A function whose own declaration says `: void` is different: returning a value from it reports "Type 'number' is not assignable to type 'void'." Note that `r` is typed `void` even though it holds 42 at runtime.

stem:
Which line reports an excess property error?

```ts
interface Cfg { port: number }

const a: () => Cfg = () => ({ port: 1, host: 'x' });                 // 1
const b: () => Cfg = () => { return { port: 1, host: 'x' }; };      // 2
const c = (): Cfg => ({ port: 1, host: 'x' });                       // 3
```

options.text: All three, because each function returns a literal with an unknown property
options.why: Only an annotated return type puts the returned literal directly against `Cfg`.

options.text: Lines 1 and 2, because the variable's function type contextually types the return
options.why: The return type is inferred from the body first, then the function types are compared.

options.text: Only line 3
options.why: The return type annotation on the arrow itself checks the returned literal.

options.text: Only line 2, because a block body with `return` is checked like a declaration
options.why: A block body behaves like the expression body here; neither is checked.

explanation: For lines 1 and 2, TypeScript infers the arrow's return type as `{ port: number; host: string }` and then checks that function type against `() => Cfg`. That is an ordinary assignability check, and extra properties are allowed, so no error. On line 3 the arrow declares `: Cfg` itself, so the returned literal is fresh against `Cfg` and tsc reports "Object literal may only specify known properties". Annotate return types when you want typo protection.
reference: TypeScript GitHub issue #241: Excess property checks for function return values

stem: Match each pair of same-named declarations in one scope with how TypeScript treats them.

options.text: Merged: the members of both are combined
options.why: Interface merging.

options.text: Error: "Duplicate identifier"
options.why: Aliases cannot be reopened.

options.text: Merged: the interface adds members to the class instance type
options.why: Class and interface merging.

options.text: Merged: the namespace adds properties to the function
options.why: Function and namespace merging.

prompts.text: `function greet() {}` and `namespace greet { export const lang = "en"; }`

explanation: TypeScript merges declarations that create compatible meanings: interfaces with interfaces, interfaces into classes, and namespaces into functions, classes or enums. This is how libraries type a function that also carries properties, such as `jQuery.ajax`. Type aliases are closed and cannot be redeclared. Class and interface merging adds types only, not runtime values.

options.text: Assignments 1 and 2, because a Dog comparer cannot compare arbitrary animals
options.why: That is the sound answer, but method syntax makes assignment 1 bivariant.

options.text: Only assignment 2
options.why: The property-syntax comparer is checked contravariantly in `T`, so the Dog version is rejected.

options.text: Only assignment 3, because a Dog array element cannot be widened to Animal
options.why: Element widening is fine; arrays of subtypes are assignable to arrays of supertypes.

options.text: None, because generic interfaces are always compared covariantly
options.why: TypeScript measures variance per type parameter from how it is used.

explanation: TypeScript measures the variance of `T` from the members. In `Cmp2`, `T` appears only in function-typed property parameters, so it is contravariant and `Cmp2<Dog>` to `Cmp2<Animal>` fails: "Type 'Cmp2<Dog>' is not assignable to type 'Cmp2<Animal>'." In `Cmp1` the member is a method, which is exempt from strictFunctionTypes, so it compiles. The same exemption is why `Array<T>` (whose methods are declared with method syntax) stays covariant.

stem: Which three tuple assignments compile under `strict: true`? (Choose three.)

options.text: `const a: [number, string?] = [1];`
options.why: An optional tuple element may be left out.

options.text: `const b: readonly [number] = [1] as [number];`
options.why: A mutable tuple is assignable to its readonly version.

options.text: `const c: [number] = [1] as readonly [number];`
options.why: Readonly to mutable fails: "The type 'readonly [number]' is 'readonly' and cannot be assigned to the mutable type '[number]'."

options.text: `const d: [number, ...string[]] = [1];`
options.why: A rest element can match zero elements.

options.text: `const e: [number, number] = [1, 2] as number[];`
options.why: Once the value is typed `number[]`, its length is unknown, so it cannot fill a fixed tuple.

explanation: Tuples follow the same rules as arrays plus length rules. Optional elements (`string?`) and rest elements (`...string[]`) relax the minimum length, so `[1]` fits both. Mutable to readonly is allowed; the reverse is not. And an assertion to `number[]` throws away the length, so it cannot be assigned to a two-element tuple: "Type 'number[]' is not assignable to type '[number, number]'."
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Optional and Rest Elements in Tuple Types
